An interactive assessment of how a shrinking cryosphere reshapes water security across 7.3 km of Himalayan relief — 2000 to 2024.

scroll to descend into the basin
01 — The Reservoir

A third of the ice is gone.

The basin’s glaciers cover 34.6% less ground than in 2000, and the loss is speeding up — from 41.5 to 56.2 km²/yr. Snow tells a subtler story: it rose, then fell. Toggle the layers and years to see the cryosphere change.

02 — Where Water Is Made

High and cold, far from anyone.

Meltwater and snow feed the northern headwaters — the dark blue on the map. It thins to almost nothing over the southern valleys where people actually live.

03 — The Twist

So is the water running out? No.

Across six epochs the supply carries no detectable trend (R²=0.086, p=0.572) — even as a third of the ice vanished. Demand rises like clockwork only because a 2%/yr growth was prescribed.

04 — Pressure

Stress swings, not slides.

Mean stress fell to 0.99 in 2010 then climbed back to 1.99 by 2024. Drag the year to watch the map breathe — and note the deepest stress always sits in the low valleys, never on the ice.

Water stress (demand ÷ availability) click to enlarge

Stress trajectory

2.31 → 0.99 (2010) → 1.99 (2024). A two-epoch study would miss the dip entirely.

05 — The Answer

What moves is the altitude.

Half the demand sits below 1,785 m; half the supply is now generated below 2,664 m. That 878 m gap is the whole finding — water isn’t vanishing, it’s being made ever higher above the people who need it.

Elevation-concentration curves · 2024

Supply (blue) sits right of demand (red). The shaded band is the displacement; widest gap D=0.34 at 2,138 m.

Separation vs stress

Narrowest 526 m in 2010 (stress 0.99); widest 878 m in 2024 (stress 1.99). Two measures, no shared arithmetic — yet they agree at both extremes.

06 — The Index & The Future

Security, mapped — and projected.

The CHWSI fuses cryosphere health and water stress into one surface: secure in the blue headwaters, vulnerable in the brown valleys. Step to 2030 to see vulnerability spread downslope.

Cryo-Hydrological Water Security Index click to enlarge

Epoch

2030 is a continuation of the trend, not a forecast — three epochs support a slope and nothing more.

The formula

CHWSI = 0.5·CHS + 0.5·(1 − Stress/5)

High = secure, low = vulnerable. Equal weights, analyst-assigned.

07 — The Verdict

Not a basin running dry — a basin whose water is climbing away from it.

The problem is geometric, not volumetric — displacement, not scarcity. Bhagirathi–Alaknanda · 18,764 km² · 446–7,804 m · HydroSHEDS L5 (PFAF 452468 + 452469). The model is simplified and SPHY-inspired — uncalibrated, unvalidated, no gauged discharge available. The two findings pressed hardest — no supply trend, and a moving separation against a fixed demand centroid — depend least on absolute magnitude and survive rescaling.
